steps.think: This is the best and the worst screen. Best: they practise what they ask, and the gap is stated plainly. Worst: a company selling agent-authority risk publishes, under its own name, content that goes live with no human review and an unprotected main branch. If my team wrote that in an audit I would open a finding.

interview.q1: A Web Summit guide for Lisbon written mostly by AI agents, with a page on each company they 'follow', every fact linked and dated. Underneath, it is RiskMandate's way of putting its three questions, reach, mandate, gap, in front of 120 companies, security and GRC first.
interview.q2: A small team, Dinis Cruz as editor-in-chief with Indi Gupte and someone called Vicky, and a set of AI agents doing the writing, reviewing and publishing. The same team works on RiskMandate. What I could not find on these screens is what RiskMandate is as a company and who owns it.
interview.q3: The facts, mostly yes: every one has a URL and a date, the article says what it does not claim and even records a 403, and the code and data are public. The framing, no more than any vendor content: by their own admission they are 'not independent of RiskMandate', the company pages come from a list with 'whether to meet' notes, and the About page says changes go live with no human review and the main branch is unprotected.
interview.q4: Nothing this week for me. I would ask our comms team to read whatever page they have on the bank and flag errors, and I might have one of my people look at the signing and the repository out of professional curiosity. If RiskMandate is at the summit I would not seek them out.
interview.q5: No, not myself. A bank answering in public what its agents can reach and who controls the gap is handing out a map of its attack surface, and under DORA that goes through our third-party and communications process, not a 15-minute chat with a vendor. I would forward it to comms to check the facts on the page, and if the email had a clear corrections address I would let them use it. The line 'Drafted by an AI agent, reviewed and sent by me' I respect; 'powered by RiskMandate' in the signature is what makes it a sales email.
interview.q6: Separate the newsroom from the sale in writing: a short, plain statement of what RiskMandate is, who owns it and pays the editors, and a promise that answers to the three questions are optional, never used for sales and can be given in general terms, plus a real corrections address on every company page. And protect your own main branch before asking me about my gap.

findings.finding: The 'INDEPENDENT ... The same team works on RiskMandate: our disclosure' box is in the first desktop screen, so the vendor tie is disclosed before any article is read.

'we are independent of Web Summit, not of RiskMandate. Read our disclosure before you weigh what we say' is stated plainly and repeated identically on the company page footer and About, which a sceptical reader checks for and finds consistent.

No screen says what RiskMandate is as a business (legal entity, owner, whether it sells to the companies covered, whether the editors are paid by it), so a reader cannot weigh the disclosure the site asks him to weigh.

The note 'The team's own notes on each company (why it matters, whether to meet, who owns it) are not published here' tells a reader that every company page is backed by a sales-style account record, which turns the page into a lead in his eyes.
'Something wrong? Tell us and we correct it' sits next to 'We publish no contact details', and no screen shows how to tell them, so the promised correction route has no visible door.

'A change to the development branch goes live with no human review first... Nothing technical stops a change to the main branch yet' is honest, but read by a CISO it is an open control gap at the very vendor asking him about his gap.
'The agent's own limits' answers reach, mandate and gap for the site's own agent before asking companies, which reads as practising what it preaches.

A '£5.00 credit' pill that drops to £4.99 on the next page and a 'This page 0.1p of 1p ... Rate it, or do not pay for it' bar are never explained on the screens read, and look like a payment mechanism to a bank reader.
'founded in Portugal (its CTO, the first employee, is listed by Web Summit from Portugal)' backs a founding fact with an inference from a speaker listing rather than a cited source.
An 'OUR PICK' tag on a vendor's session contradicts 'Nothing on it is an endorsement' two screens later, with no stated basis for the pick.
'If you are at Feedzai, the quickest way to get this right is to tell us how it works' reads as a request for product internals, which a security or fraud company will not give in public.

'WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM', including 'did not list Henna Virkkunen' and the EUIPO '403 on 5 November', shows the limits of the sourcing and is what moved this reader from suspicion to provisional trust in the facts.
'Who made this' lists an agent writer, an agent reviewer and an agent publisher with no human named as having read the article before it went live.
A source given as 'S2, desks/curator/README.md' is an internal file path that a reader cannot open or interpret.
The editor is 'Vicky' on About and the front page but 'Vicky Wang' in bylines and the company page footer, an inconsistency a reader checking who is behind the site notices.
The key that signs articles 'dies with the session', and no screen says how a reader verifies a signature after that.
Public source code, data as JSON, a release history and a version on every page give a technical reader something he can audit himself.
'Registration: collect your lanyard and wristband' repeats for each day and place in the agenda column, crowding out everything else on desktop and phone.
On the phone the 'INDEPENDENT ... our disclosure' box is absent from the first screen, so the only ownership signal a phone reader gets is 'Powered by RiskMandate'.
The floating 'Ask' button covers text on every phone screen read, including the first of the three questions and a source's 'read' date.
The company graph on the phone has labels too small to read and one truncated ('The Hacking Ga...').
The same long websummit.com session URL is printed three times in one phone screen, breaking the text into hexadecimal fragments.
